opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've been noticing more over the last few years, and I don't fully have it figured out. I grew up pretty secular, and for a long time my sense was that rationality, effective altruism, and caring about the world were enough of a framework. In some ways they were. They gave me a community, a sense of purpose, a way to orient toward big questions.

As I've gotten older, I've started to feel the limits of that. A lot of what I do professionally is thinking about AI risk and forecasting, staring at the possibility that the world could change radically, maybe catastrophically, within my lifetime. That's heavy. The intellectual frameworks I have are good at telling me what might happen and what to do about it. They're less good at helping me *live* with it, at giving me rituals, a sense of continuity, or a way to sit with uncertainty and grief that isn't just more analysis.

So part of what I mean by a "religion-shaped thing" is practices more than beliefs. Religions bundle together community that shows up week after week regardless of what's going on in your career, markers for life transitions, an explicit space for gratitude and mourning, and a tradition older than you that you're participating in. I look at that bundle and think: that's actually a sophisticated technology for being human, and I've mostly been doing without it.

There's also something about time horizons. When you're younger, you can run on ambition and novelty. As you age, you think more about what sustains you over decades, how you want to raise kids or show up for people, what you want your days to feel like, not just what you want to accomplish. A purely consequentialist lens can make everything feel instrumental. I want some part of my life that isn't instrumental, that's just about reverence or connection for its own sake.

I don't think that means I'll suddenly adopt a set of metaphysical beliefs I don't hold. But I've become much less dismissive of what traditions have figured out, and more curious whether I can find or build something that gives me that structure while staying honest with myself about what I actually believe. I'm still very much in the exploring phase.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I'm not religious and I don't think I'm going to become religious in the sense of actually believing in God or an afterlife. The desire isn't really about metaphysics. It's about the shape of a life, and I've only started noticing this in the last few years.

When I was in my early twenties, I think I had a kind of implicit assumption that the thing you get from religion, you can just reconstruct piece by piece from secular stuff. You get community from your friends and your workplace, you get meaning from your projects, you get moral guidance from thinking hard about ethics. And I still believe each of those pieces is available. But what I've come to appreciate is that religions bundle them together in a way that's actually really hard to replicate à la carte.

So a few concrete things. One is ritual, and specifically ritual that's not up to me. I'm the kind of person who, if left to my own devices, will optimize everything, including my own rest and reflection, and that optimization tends to eat the thing it's supposed to protect. The appeal of something like a Sabbath is precisely that it's a rule you didn't make and can't renegotiate with yourself at 11pm on a Friday because there's one more email. I notice that the secular versions I've tried, like "I'll do a weekly reflection," just quietly decay, because the only authority behind them is me, and I'm an unreliable enforcer.

A second thing is a community that's organized around something other than being interesting or successful. A lot of my life is in the effective altruism and AI safety world, and I love those communities, but they're selected for a very particular kind of person and the implicit social currency is intellectual contribution. A church, at its best, has eighty-year-olds and toddlers and people who are going through a divorce, and the premise is just that you show up and you're a member. I think as I get older and start thinking about things like having kids and about my parents aging, that kind of thick, intergenerational, non-meritocratic community looks a lot more valuable than it did when I was twenty-four and mostly wanted to find the smartest people in the room.

And then the third thing, which is maybe the hardest to talk about, is some structured way of relating to grief and mortality and the fact that you don't control most of what happens. I spend a lot of my professional life thinking about really large-scale, high-variance outcomes, and I think it's actually psychologically corrosive to hold "the fate of the world might be decided in the next decade and I have some small lever on it" without any counterweight. Religions have a lot of accumulated technology for holding both seriousness and acceptance at the same time, for saying this matters enormously and also you are small and it is not all on you. I find myself wanting that technology even though I don't buy the story it comes packaged in.

So where that leaves me is a sort of awkward in-between. I've looked at things like secular congregations and Unitarian stuff, and they tend to feel a little thin to me, like they kept the form and lost the gravity. But I've also become more sympathetic to people who are, for lack of a better word, religious for instrumental reasons, who participate because of what it does for their life and hold the metaphysics loosely. I used to think that was a bit intellectually dishonest. Now I think it might just be a reasonable adult response to the fact that we evolved to live inside these structures and modernity sort of dissolved them without replacing them. I don't have a resolution. It's mostly something I notice as an itch that's gotten stronger, and that I think a lot of people in my cohort are quietly feeling too.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is wanting a way to connect what I believe matters with how I actually live day to day. You can have this very abstract commitment to making the world better, but that doesn’t automatically give you rituals, or community, or a way to process grief and uncertainty.

And as I get older, I feel more drawn to those things—to having practices that help me step back from whatever I’m anxious about that day and remember what I care about. And to doing that with other people, rather than treating it as an individual project of getting my beliefs and habits right.

I don’t think that desire itself gives me a reason to believe any particular religious claim. But I do think it points to something that’s easy to underestimate if you primarily think of religion as a set of propositions. There’s also the question of how you sustain a meaningful life together, including when things are hard and you don’t have answers. That’s the part I find myself wanting more of.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that I’ve become more aware of the gap between having a set of beliefs and having a way of living. You can have views about what matters, and you can reason about what you should do, but that doesn’t necessarily give you practices that help you actually feel those things or act on them consistently.

And the religion-shaped thing would bring together a few things that otherwise feel quite separate: community, ritual, a place to bring grief or gratitude, and some shared commitment to becoming better people. A community where you’re not just getting together because you happen to enjoy the same activity, but where you have obligations to each other.

I don’t think getting older has made me feel like I can choose to believe something because it would be comforting. But it has made me take those needs more seriously. I’m less inclined to assume that if you have the right arguments and good friendships, everything else will take care of itself.
